components.note: 十 (ten, suggesting abundance) — relates to 华's meaning 'flowery, splendid,' an abundance of blossoms.
化 (huà) gives a sound hint — 华 is pronounced huá, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
皿 (dish) — 盛 relates to filling a dish or vessel to abundance.
成 (chéng) gives a sound distantly related to shèng, having drifted apart over time.
页 (head) — 顿 originally related to bowing the head, i.e. a pause or stop
屯 (tún) gives a sound distantly related to 顿's reading dùn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 乔治·华盛顿是美国的第一位总统。
example.pinyin: Qiáozhì Huáshèngdùn shì Měiguó de dìyī wèi zǒngtǒng.
example.english: George Washington was the first president of the United States.
example.fact: 华盛顿 is the standard Mandarin transliteration for the name/place "Washington" — built by choosing characters purely for their sound (华 huá, 盛 shèng, 顿 dùn) rather than their literal meaning ("splendid", "abundant", "pause"), the same phonetic-borrowing strategy behind 乔治 ("George", also in this batch, rank 1221).

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姐 names a female relative, an older sister.
且 (qiě) gives the rhyme, close to jiě though the tone differs.
女 (woman) — 妹 names a female relative, a younger sister.
未 (wèi) gives a rhyme close to mèi, with a different initial.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì hǎo jiěmèi.
example.english: We are close sisters.
example.fact: 姐妹 strings together "older sister" (姐) and "younger sister" (妹) into one word covering "sisters" as a group, regardless of birth order — the same additive strategy behind 兄弟 ("brothers", elder brother + younger brother), since Chinese kinship terms build outward from specific relative ages rather than one generic "sibling" word.

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual/spirits) — 神 relates to gods and spirits.
申 (shēn) gives a hint of the sound — 神 is pronounced shén, a connection that has shifted over time.
禾 (grain) — an older sense of 秘 was linked to grain kept out of sight, before it narrowed to 'secret.'
必 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 秘.

example.pinyin: Zhège dǎoyǔ fēicháng shénmì.
example.english: This island is very mysterious.
example.fact: 神 ("god, spirit") combines with 秘 ("secret") to give 神秘 an almost otherworldly sense of hidden secrecy; 秘 itself, per its own semantic component 禾 ("grain"), is traditionally linked to grain once kept out of sight, before the character's meaning narrowed to just "secret."

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 他终于把自己的梦想实现了。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú bǎ zìjǐ de mèngxiǎng shíxiàn le.
example.english: He finally made his own dream a reality.
example.fact: 现 (built from 见 "to see" catching sight of a valuable 王/玉 "jade") contributes a sense of "to appear, to manifest" — 实现 pairs "to make real" with "to manifest," capturing the idea of turning something abstract, like a plan or a dream, into a visible reality.

components.note: 目 (eye) shows 瞧 relates to looking or seeing.
焦 (jiāo) gives a sound distantly related to qiáo, having drifted apart in the initial consonant over time.
目 (eye) shows 瞧 relates to looking or seeing.
焦 (jiāo) gives a sound distantly related to qiáo, having drifted apart in the initial consonant over time.

example.pinyin: Nǐ lái qiáoqiao zhège dōngxi.
example.english: Come take a look at this thing.
example.fact: 瞧瞧 doubles the verb 瞧 ("to look") the same way 谢谢 doubles 谢 ("to thank") — reduplicating a one-syllable action verb like this makes it sound light and casual, "just a quick look," with the second syllable typically toneless in speech.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick, action) — 政 relates to administering or governing.
正 (zhèng) gives the sound — 政 is also pronounced zhèng, an exact match.
氵 (water) — 治 relates to managing or controlling the flow of water, such as flood control.
台 (a platform, structure) — a structure used to direct and control water gave 治 its meaning 'to govern' or 'to manage.'

example.pinyin: Tā duì zhèngzhì hěn gǎn xìngqù.
example.english: He is very interested in politics.
example.fact: 政 (attaching 攵, "a hand with a rod," to 正, "correct, upright") pictures enforcing correct order by force — governing — while 治 (water 氵 plus a platform 台) originally meant directing a river's flow; 政治 fuses "governing people" with "managing, controlling" into the modern word for "politics."

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient texts were written on bound bamboo strips, and 第 originally referred to the sequential order of such strips, giving rise to its meaning 'ordinal number' (as in 第一, first).
囗 (an enclosure) — 四 pictures a bounded space.
儿 (a person) — a person enclosed within four walls gave 四 its meaning 'four,' though the exact link to the number is debated.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒmen dìsì cì jiànmiàn.
example.english: This is the fourth time we've met.
example.fact: 第 attaches to a bare cardinal number to build an ordinal (第一 "first", 第二 "second", 第四 "fourth") — without 第, 四 alone just means the cardinal "four," so this one small character is doing all of the "-th" work in a Chinese ordinal.

components.note: 鬼 (ghost) — 魔 names a demon or evil spirit.
麻 (má) gives a sound distantly related to mó, having drifted apart over time.
The 田-shaped top pictures a large, strange head.
儿-shaped legs below trace a crouching, spindly body, together giving 鬼 the shape of a ghostly figure.

example.hanzi: 他在梦里看到一个魔鬼。
example.pinyin: Tā zài mèng lǐ kàndào yí gè móguǐ.
example.english: He saw a devil in his dream.
example.fact: 魔 is itself built on top of 鬼 ("ghost, spirit") — 魔鬼 stacks two already-supernatural characters into one word, the same reinforcing strategy behind 喜欢 ("to like", stacking two "joy" characters); 鬼's own shape, a strange 田-like head over spindly 儿-like legs, is a fairly literal picture of a ghostly figure.

components.note: 子 (child) — 孤 originally described a child without a parent, an orphan.
瓜 (guā) gives a sound close to gū, sharing the same initial.
犭 (dog) — an old link behind 独's meaning 'alone, single, solitary'
虫 (chóng) gives a loose sound connection to 独's reading dú

example.pinyin: Lǎorén yí gè rén zhù, hěn gūdú.
example.english: The old man lives alone; he is very lonely.
example.fact: 孤 originally named a fatherless child, an orphan (built from 子 "child" with the phonetic 瓜), while 独 carries a sense of "single, solitary"; 孤独 combines "orphaned" with "alone" into today's word for the emotional state of loneliness, not just physical solitude.

components.note: 冂 (an enclosure or doorway) — 内 pictures the space one enters.
人 (person) — a person entering an enclosure gave 内 its meaning 'inside' or 'within.'
宀 (roof/house) — 容's meaning 'to contain, hold' relates to a house holding things, extended to 'appearance, to allow, tolerate.'

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū de nèiróng hěn yǒuqù.
example.english: The content of this book is very interesting.
example.fact: 容 on its own already means "to hold, to contain" (built from 宀, "roof," the image of a house holding things inside) — 内容 pairs that "container" sense with 内 ("inside") to literally mean "what is held inside," giving the word its modern sense of "content."

components.note: 巨 depicts a hand gripping a large carpenter's square, a tool for measuring right angles — an image linked to great size, giving 巨 its meaning 'huge, giant.'
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.pinyin: Zhè kē shù fēicháng jùdà.
example.english: This tree is enormous.
example.fact: 巨 and 大 both independently mean roughly "big, great" — 巨大 doubles up two near-synonyms for size into one intensified adjective, the same word-building strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该; 巨 itself is traditionally read as a picture of a hand gripping an oversized carpenter's square.

components.note: 宀 (a roof) — a house where valuables are kept
玉 (jade) — the treasure kept safe inside
宀 (a roof) — a house where valuables are kept
玉 (jade) — the treasure kept safe inside

example.pinyin: Māma bàozhe bǎobao.
example.english: Mom is holding the baby.
example.fact: 宝 originally meant "treasure" (a roof 宀 sheltering jade 玉 inside) — reduplicating it into 宝宝 turns a noun for a precious object into an affectionate term for a baby or loved one, the same doubling pattern seen in 谢谢 and 瞧瞧, just applied to a noun instead of a verb.

components.note: Heart/mind — punishment is meant to affect one's conscience.
Gives the sound zhēng, related to chéng but drifted apart over time.
罒 (a net) — historically linked to wrongdoing and being caught out.
刂 (a knife/blade) — carrying out punishment, together giving 罚 its meaning 'to punish, penalize.'

example.hanzi: 迟到的学生被老师惩罚了。
example.pinyin: Chídào de xuésheng bèi lǎoshī chéngfá le.
example.english: The students who were late were punished by the teacher.
example.fact: 惩 carries the heart radical 心, tying punishment to its effect on one's conscience, while 罚's components (a net 罒 plus a blade 刂) point to catching wrongdoing and carrying out a penalty — together 惩罚 layers the psychological and the punitive sides of punishment into one word.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 价格加上运费一共一百元。
example.pinyin: Jiàgé jiāshàng yùnfèi yígòng yìbǎi yuán.
example.english: The price plus shipping comes to one hundred yuan in total.
example.fact: 加 pictures adding one's physical strength (力) together with supportive words (口) — literally "muscle plus voice" — while 上 here works as a directional complement meaning "on top of, additionally"; 加上 stacks "to add" onto "on top" to introduce one more item or reason, much like English "plus" or "on top of that."

meanings: (lit. and fig.) to open a door

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
门 is a picture of a double-leafed door or gate, drawn symmetrically to show two swinging panels.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn jǐ diǎn kāimén?
example.english: What time does this shop open?
example.fact: 开门 extends beyond its literal sense of unlatching a door to mean "opening for business" — the moment a shop's actual door swings open each day stands in for the more abstract idea of a business being open, a very physical image (per 开's own etymology, hands 廾 lifting away a latch 一) doing double duty.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 蓝 originally named the indigo plant used to make blue dye.
监 (jiān) gives a sound distantly related to lán, having drifted apart over time.
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan lánsè de tiānkōng.
example.english: He likes the blue sky.
example.fact: 蓝 originally named the indigo plant itself (built from 艹, "grass, plant") before it came to mean the blue color extracted from it — a dye-plant's name becoming the color word, the same shift English makes when "orange" the color takes its name from the fruit.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 退 relates to moving backward or away
艮 (gèn) gives a sound distantly related to 退's reading tuì, having drifted apart over time
屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.pinyin: Tā juédìng tuìchū bǐsài.
example.english: He decided to withdraw from the competition.
example.fact: 退 (辶 "to walk" plus the phonetic 艮) pictures physically moving backward, while 出 pictures a sprout growing up and out of a container; 退出 combines "stepping back" with "going out," making it equally natural for leaving a competition, an organization, or, in modern usage, logging out of an app.

components.note: The 田-shaped top pictures a large, strange head.
儿-shaped legs below trace a crouching, spindly body, together giving 鬼 the shape of a ghostly figure.
鬼 (ghost/spirit) — 魂 names a person's spirit or soul.
云 (yún) gives a rhyme close to hún, with a different initial.

example.hanzi: 她说这栋房子里有鬼魂。
example.pinyin: Tā shuō zhè dòng fángzi lǐ yǒu guǐhún.
example.english: She says there's a ghost in this house.
example.fact: 魂 is literally built on top of 鬼 ("ghost") itself, with 云 ("cloud") lending only its sound — 鬼魂 pairs the picture-word for "ghost" with the more abstract "soul, spirit," reflecting the old folk belief that a person's 魂 could linger on as a 鬼 after death.

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ de wǎngqiú duìshǒu.
example.english: He is my tennis opponent.
example.fact: 对 carries a core sense of "facing, matching, corresponding to" (from two hands meeting) — 对手 literally means "a matching hand," the person whose skill is set directly against yours, whether in sport, business, or debate.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.

example.pinyin: Jūnduì jìxù qiánjìn.
example.english: The army continued to advance.
example.fact: 进 (辶 "to walk" plus the phonetic 井) already means "to advance, to enter" on its own — 前进 reinforces it by adding 前 ("forward, ahead"), the same reinforcing-synonym pattern seen in 喜欢 and 巨大, just built from two motion-related characters instead.

components.note: 夭 depicts a person leaning to one side, arms swinging — here the pose of walking high up on stilts, giving 乔 its meaning 'tall, lofty.'
氵 (water) — 治 relates to managing or controlling the flow of water, such as flood control.
台 (a platform, structure) — a structure used to direct and control water gave 治 its meaning 'to govern' or 'to manage.'

example.hanzi: 乔治是一个很常见的英文名字。
example.pinyin: Qiáozhì shì yí gè hěn chángjiàn de Yīngwén míngzi.
example.english: George is a very common English name.
example.fact: 乔治 is a pure sound-based transliteration of the English name "George," pairing 乔 (whose own etymology pictures someone walking tall on stilts, "lofty") with 治 ("to govern") — chosen purely for their pronunciation, not their meaning, the same phonetic strategy behind 华盛顿 ("Washington," rank 1201 in this batch).

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual/spirits) — 神 relates to gods and spirits.
申 (shēn) gives a hint of the sound — 神 is pronounced shén, a connection that has shifted over time.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a rider.
可 here is said to depict a mount — a person riding in an unusual way gave 奇 its meaning 'strange, odd, remarkable.'

example.pinyin: Dàzìrán zhēn shì shénqí.
example.english: Nature is truly magical.
example.fact: 神 ("god, spirit") pairs with 奇 ("strange, remarkable" — traditionally pictured as someone riding in an unusual way) to describe something so remarkable it feels touched by the divine; 神奇 reads as more wondrous and awe-struck than the more hidden, secretive 神秘 ("mysterious," also in this batch, rank 1203), even though both start with the same 神.

components.note: 牛 (ox) on the left is the animal being tended.
攵 (a hand holding a stick) on the right shows someone driving or herding it, giving 牧 its meaning 'to herd, to tend livestock.'
帀 (a banner or covering) — flying above the scene.
刂 (a knife) — wielded with skill beneath the banner, an image of expertise giving 师 its meaning 'master, teacher, expert.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì zhège jiàotáng de mùshī.
example.english: He is the pastor of this church.
example.fact: 牧 pictures a hand with a stick (攵) driving an ox (牛) — literally "herding" — extended metaphorically in 牧师 to a religious leader who "shepherds" a congregation, echoing the same herder/flock metaphor English uses for "pastor" (from Latin pastor, "shepherd").

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
纟 (thread) — 级 originally named a strand or rank of silk thread, extended to 'grade, level, rank.'
及 (jí) gives the sound — 级 is also pronounced jí, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒ nǚ'ér xiànzài shàng sān niánjí.
example.english: My daughter is now in third grade.
example.fact: 级, whose thread radical 纟 originally named a rank or strand of silk, extends that "strand/rank" image in 年级 — literally "year-rank" — to name the specific step of schooling a student has reached in a given year.

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, jade) — 环 originally referred to a round jade ring or bracelet
不 (bù) gives a sound distantly related to 环's reading huán, having drifted apart considerably over time
土 (earth) — 境 relates to land and territory, extended to mean 'environment, boundary'
竟 (jìng) gives the sound — 境 is also pronounced jìng, an exact match

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi bǎohù huánjìng.
example.english: We should protect the environment.
example.fact: 环 originally named a round jade ring or bracelet (built from 王, a variant of 玉, "jade") — extended metaphorically to anything that encircles, 环境 combines that "surrounding ring" image with 境 ("territory, boundary") to give the modern word for one's surrounding environment or circumstances.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 提 relates to lifting or carrying something by hand.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 提 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.pinyin: Tā zài xìn lǐ tídào nǐ le.
example.english: He mentioned you in the letter.
example.fact: 提 (a hand 扌 lifting something up) contributes the image of "raising, bringing up," while 到 means "to arrive, to reach" — 提到 literally "raises [a topic] until it arrives [in the conversation]," a fairly direct compositional route to the abstract sense of "to mention."

components.note: 禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī gǒu shì zázhǒng.
example.english: This dog is a mixed breed.
example.fact: 种 (grain 禾 plus the phonetic 中) literally means "seed, to plant" — 杂种 literally "mixed seed," a term from breeding and agriculture for a cross-bred animal or plant; that same literal "mixed seed" image is also what gives the word its much harsher, vulgar insult sense in modern slang, a jump in register worth knowing before using it casually.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 刺 describes the action of piercing or stabbing with something sharp.
朿 (cì) gives the sound — an exact match with 刺's reading cì.
氵 (water) — 激 originally described water dashing or surging forcefully
敫 (jiǎo) gives a sound distantly related to 激's reading jī, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 蹦极是一项很刺激的运动。
example.pinyin: Bèngjí shì yí xiàng hěn cìjī de yùndòng.
example.english: Bungee jumping is a very thrilling sport.
example.fact: 刺 pictures a blade 刂 piercing something sharp (its phonetic 朿 is an exact sound match for cì) — 刺激 combines "to prick, to stab" with 激 ("water surging forcefully") into one word that covers both the negative sense of "to provoke, to irritate" and the more neutral or positive sense of "to stimulate, to thrill," depending on context.

components.note: Originally depicted a hand 扌 gripping a weapon 戈; this original meaning was later borrowed to represent the pronoun 'I/we.'
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ huì nǔlì xuéxí Zhōngwén.
example.english: I will study Chinese hard.
example.fact: 会 alone already carries two distinct senses that 我会 inherits directly depending on context — a learned ability ("I know how to," as in 我会说中文, "I can speak Chinese") and a prediction about intention or the future ("I will," as in this example) — the same verb doing quite different grammatical jobs depending on what follows it.

components.note: 见 (to see) — 规 originally named a craftsman's compass, a tool used to observe and measure circles, extended to 'rule, regulation.'
夫 (fū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from guī.
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.pinyin: Gōngsī yǒu yángé de guīdìng.
example.english: The company has strict regulations.
example.fact: 规 originally named a compass, a craftsman's tool for drawing perfect circles (linked to 见, "to see, observe") — 规定 combines that tool-for-precision image with 定 ("to fix, to settle") to describe rules that have been measured out and fixed in place.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.pinyin: Tā yǒu hǎoduō péngyou.
example.english: He has a lot of friends.
example.fact: 好 here isn't its usual sense of "good" but works instead as an intensifier before 多 ("much, many"), similar to how colloquial English "a good many" uses "good" the same non-literal way — one of several set phrases (好久 "quite a while", 好几 "quite a few") where 好 means "quite, very" rather than "good."

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.

example.hanzi: 警长带领警察调查这个案子。
example.pinyin: Jǐngzhǎng dàilǐng jǐngchá diàochá zhège ànzi.
example.english: The police chief led the officers in investigating this case.
example.fact: 长, here read zhǎng rather than the more common cháng ("long"), keeps its older sense of "chief, head, elder" — the same reading shows up in 校长 ("school principal"), 部长 ("department head"), and 家长 ("parent, head of household"), a whole family of "-长" leadership titles built the same way.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 最 pictures something happening under the sun, that is, everywhere.
取 (to take, gather) — combined with the sun above, gathering everything under the sun gave 最 its meaning of 'most' or 'the utmost.'
亻 (person) shows 佳 describes a positive quality, often applied to people or things.
圭 (guī) gives a sound distantly related to jiā, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这是解决问题的最佳方法。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì jiějué wèntí de zuìjiā fāngfǎ.
example.english: This is the best way to solve the problem.
example.fact: 最 (built from 日 "sun" over 取 "to take, gather") pictures gathering everything under the sun — a natural superlative prefix for "-est, most" — combined here with 佳 ("fine, excellent," a quality more often applied to people or achievements) to give a somewhat more formal, written-register "best" than the everyday 最好.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài xúnzhǎo shòuhàirén.
example.english: The police are searching for the victim.
example.fact: 受 (two hands, one giving 爫 and one receiving 又, passing something between them) contributes the sense of "to receive, to suffer," which 受害人 combines with 害 ("harm") and 人 ("person") into a fully transparent term: literally "a person who has received harm."

components.note: 发 (fā) gives a sound related to fèi, sharing the initial f-, though the rhyme has drifted from ā to èi over time.
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.pinyin: Bié shuō fèihuà le, kuài diǎn zuòshì.
example.english: Stop talking nonsense, hurry up and get to work.
example.fact: 废 ("useless, abolished") plus 话 ("words, speech" — built from 讠 "speech" and 舌 "tongue") combine literally into "useless words"; 废话 also doubles as a sarcastic retort in speech ("废话!", roughly "No duh! Obviously!") when someone states something painfully obvious.

components.note: 攵 (an action/to strike) — 效 relates to the result produced by an action
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to 效's reading xiào
田 (here representing round fruit, not its usual meaning 'field') — 果 pictures fruit hanging from branches.
木 (tree) — fruit growing on a tree gave 果 its meaning 'fruit' and, more broadly, 'result.'

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yào de xiàoguǒ hěn hǎo.
example.english: This medicine is very effective.
example.fact: 果 ("fruit hanging from a tree," extended to "result") recurs across several common words for outcomes — 效果 ("effect"), 结果 ("result"), 如果 ("if", literally "as the result [would be]") — all built on the same underlying "fruit leads to result" metaphor, so recognizing 果 helps a learner guess the general sense of a whole family of words.

components.note: 口 is a simple picture of an open mouth.

example.hanzi: 医生正在处理他的伤口。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng zhèngzài chǔlǐ tā de shāngkǒu.
example.english: The doctor is treating his wound.
example.fact: 口 ("mouth," a simple picture of an open mouth) extends metaphorically in 伤口 to describe the "opening" a wound makes in the skin — the same "opening = mouth" metaphor appears in 门口 ("doorway," literally "gate mouth") and 河口 ("river mouth, estuary").

components.note: 鬼 (ghost) — 魔 names a demon or evil spirit.
麻 (má) gives a sound distantly related to mó, having drifted apart over time.
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 这个故事里的魔法非常神奇。
example.pinyin: Zhège gùshi lǐ de mófǎ fēicháng shénqí.
example.english: The magic in this story is truly wondrous.
example.fact: 法 (water 氵 flowing along a fixed course 去) originally meant "law, method" — the idea that even magic follows its own hidden rules; 魔法 pairs "demon, spirit" (魔, built on 鬼 "ghost") with that "method" sense, framing magic as a supernatural technique rather than pure chaos.

components.note: 犭 (dog) — an old link behind 独's meaning 'alone, single, solitary'
虫 (chóng) gives a loose sound connection to 独's reading dú
A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan dúzì sànbù.
example.english: He likes to take walks by himself.
example.fact: 独自 doubles down on solitude by combining 独 ("alone, single" — its dog radical 犭 comes from an old association between a lone dog and solitary living) with 自 ("self," itself a pictograph of a nose, since ancient Chinese speakers pointed at their own nose to mean "me") — two independently "alone/self"-flavored characters reinforcing each other.

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'
金 depicts a bell or metal casting mold, with dots representing droplets of molten metal — a picture linked to metal and, later, specifically gold.

example.pinyin: Qǐng yòng xiànjīn zhīfù.
example.english: Please pay with cash.
example.fact: 现 contributes its "to appear, to be present" sense (from 见, "to see") to 现金, literally "money that is present, on hand right now" — distinguishing physical, immediately available cash from money that exists only as a number in an account or a future payment.

meanings: to understand sth well and know how to use it

components.note: 手 (hand) — 掌 names the palm, part of the hand.
尚 (shàng) gives a rhyme close to zhǎng, with the initial shifted.
扌 (hand) — 握 describes an action done with the hand: grasping tightly.
屋 (wū) gives a sound distantly related to wò, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这项技能他已经掌握了。
example.pinyin: Zhè xiàng jìnéng tā yǐjīng zhǎngwò le.
example.english: He has already mastered this skill.
example.fact: 掌 names the palm of the hand, and 握 means "to grip tightly" — 掌握 literally "palm plus grip," a vivid image of physically holding something firmly in one's hand that extends metaphorically to mentally "grasping" a skill, a language, or a situation.

components.note: 龶-shaped top pictures a ripe stalk of grain.
夂 below pictures roots or a foot, together giving 麦 its meaning 'wheat.'
十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 请检查一下麦克有没有声音。
example.pinyin: Qǐng jiǎnchá yíxià màikè yǒu méiyǒu shēngyīn.
example.english: Please check whether the microphone has sound.
example.fact: 麦克 is a truncated, purely phonetic loanword — short for the fuller transliteration 麦克风 (màikèfēng, from English "microphone") — the same kind of clipping English does when it shortens "microphone" to "mic," just borrowed sound-by-sound into characters that otherwise mean "wheat" (麦) and "to overcome" (克).

components.note: 儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.
立 (standing) — a small figure standing upright.
里 here representing a village or settlement, together giving 童 its meaning 'child.'

example.hanzi: 这个公园有儿童游乐区。
example.pinyin: Zhège gōngyuán yǒu értóng yóulèqū.
example.english: This park has a children's play area.
example.fact: 儿童 is the neutral, written-register word for "child" — used in official contexts like 儿童节 ("Children's Day") — while 孩子 is the everyday spoken word for the same thing; 儿 by itself is a simple picture of a small child, drawn with an oversized head on a small body.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
子 (child) — 孩 relates directly to children
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to 孩's reading hái
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 那个女孩子在公园里跳舞。
example.pinyin: Nàge nǚháizi zài gōngyuán lǐ tiàowǔ.
example.english: That girl is dancing in the park.
example.fact: 女孩子 spells out "female child" in full by stacking 女 ("woman, female" — a pictograph of a kneeling, arms-crossed figure) directly onto 孩子 ("child"), where casual speech often just shortens it to 女孩 without the light final 子.

components.note: 弓 (bow) — a strong bow that took great force to draw gave 强 its meaning 'strong, powerful.'
虫 was a different phonetic element historically; its pronunciation has shifted so far from qiáng over time that the sound link is no longer obvious.
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.hanzi: 这个国家的军队非常强大。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā de jūnduì fēicháng qiángdà.
example.english: This country's military is very powerful.
example.fact: 强 (a bow 弓 strong enough to require great force to draw) pairs with 大 ("big," a person standing with arms and legs spread wide) into 强大, a word usually reserved for large-scale power — countries, armies, economies — rather than an individual's physical strength, which Chinese more often describes with 强壮.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.hanzi: 他们决定分开一段时间。
example.pinyin: Tāmen juédìng fēnkāi yí duàn shíjiān.
example.english: They decided to separate for a while.
example.fact: 分 (a knife 刀 cutting something already split 八) contributes "to divide," while 开 contributes "open, apart" (two hands 廾 lifting away a door's latch 一); 分开 combines "cutting apart" with "opening apart" into the general verb for separating two things, whether physical objects, a couple, or ideas.

components.note: 承 depicts multiple hands supporting and lifting something from below — giving 承 its meaning 'to support, to receive, to inherit.'
讠 (speech) — 诺 relates to a spoken promise or agreement.
若 (ruò) gives a rhyme close to nuò, sharing a related initial.

example.hanzi: 他没有实现自己的承诺。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu shíxiàn zìjǐ de chéngnuò.
example.english: He didn't fulfill his own promise.
example.fact: 承 (multiple hands supporting something from below) contributes "to receive, to bear," while 诺 (speech 讠 plus the phonetic 若) names a spoken "yes, agreed" — 承诺 literally "to bear a spoken yes," framing a promise as a weight one agrees to carry, not just words spoken lightly.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 脖 names a body part, the neck.
孛 (bèi) gives a sound close to bó, sharing the same initial.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Chángjǐnglù de bózi hěn cháng.
example.english: A giraffe's neck is very long.
example.fact: 脖 carries the flesh radical ⺼ (a variant of 肉, "meat"), marking it as a body-part word, paired with the light noun suffix 子 also seen in 孩子 and 女孩子 elsewhere in this batch — the same suffix pattern that turns a bound root into an everyday, free-standing noun.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 检 originally related to a wooden tally or label used for checking records
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 检's reading jiǎn, having drifted apart over time
宀 (roof) — 察 relates to careful observation
祭 (jì) gives a loose sound connection to 察's reading chá

example.pinyin: Jiǎncháguān zài fǎtíng shàng fāyán.
example.english: The prosecutor spoke in court.
example.fact: 检 (originally a wooden tally used for checking records, from 木 "wood") and 察 (careful observation, under a roof 宀) both independently mean "to inspect, to examine" — 检察官 stacks two near-synonymous "to examine" characters onto 官 ("official") to name the official whose job is examining evidence and prosecuting a case.

meanings: (of a movie, book, TV show etc) good

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo qúnzi hěn hǎokàn.
example.english: This skirt looks very nice.
example.fact: 好看 literally combines "good" with "to look" (看, pictured as a hand 手 shading the eyes 目 to see into the distance) into "good to look at" — parallel to 好吃 ("good to eat, tasty") and 好听 ("good to listen to, pleasant-sounding"), a small family of "好 + sense-verb" adjectives covering different senses.
